speakerBio: A clinical microbiologist and infection-control lead who reads antibiograms for pleasure and insists that naming the exact resistance mechanism is the first act of treating it.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 61-year-old returns to your ICU three weeks after an abdominal operation abroad, now in septic shock from a urinary source. The lab phones: the blood culture is a Gram-negative rod, and the rapid molecular panel has flagged a carbapenemase gene. Your standard 'big gun' — meropenem — will not work. In that moment the whole conference converges: you need to know the enemy, its mechanism of resistance, and which of the newer agents can still kill it. This session is a field guide to the multidrug-resistant organisms and the drugs that remain.

1 · Know the mechanisms — four ways bacteria defeat antibiotics 🛡️

Every resistance phenotype reduces to a handful of molecular tricks. Learn the mechanism and the drug choices become logical, not memorised.

MechanismHow it worksClassic example
Enzymatic destructionThe bug makes an enzyme that cleaves the drug — β-lactamases hydrolyse the β-lactam ringESBLs, AmpC, carbapenemases (KPC, NDM, OXA)
Target modificationThe drug's binding site is altered so it no longer fitsMRSA (altered PBP2a via mecA); VRE (D-Ala-D-Lac cell wall); macrolide erm
Efflux pumpsMembrane pumps actively export the drug before it actsPseudomonas, Acinetobacter (multi-drug efflux)
Reduced permeability / porin lossThe bug closes the outer-membrane channels the drug uses to enterCarbapenem resistance in Enterobacterales via porin loss + AmpC/ESBL
💡 Pearl

Carbapenem resistance often needs two hits — e.g. an ESBL/AmpC plus porin loss, or a true carbapenemase. That is why a lab may report an organism as carbapenem-resistant without detecting a carbapenemase gene: the mechanism can be permeability, not an enzyme.

2 · The β-lactamase family tree — ESBL, AmpC, carbapenemase 🌳

ESBL — Extended-Spectrum β-Lactamase

Plasmid-encoded enzymes (CTX-M, TEM, SHV) that hydrolyse penicillins, and crucially the 3rd-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, ceftazidime) and aztreonam. Typically in E. coli and Klebsiella. Inhibited by clavulanate in vitro, but the reliable clinical answer for serious infection is a carbapenem.

  • Serious/bacteraemic ESBL infection → carbapenem (meropenem, ertapenem). The MERINO trial showed piperacillin–tazobactam was inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia — so do not rely on pip-tazo for serious ESBL disease.
  • Cefepime may be used only if the MIC is low and the infection non-severe — it is not a dependable ESBL agent at higher MICs.
  • Uncomplicated ESBL cystitis can often be treated orally (nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin) — spare the carbapenem.

AmpC — the inducible chromosomal enzyme

Chromosomal (sometimes plasmid) β-lactamase in the "SPACE/ESCPM" organisms — Serratia, Pseudomonas/Providencia, Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Morganella. It can be de-repressed (induced) under β-lactam pressure, so an organism that looks susceptible on day 1 can become resistant to 3rd-gen cephalosporins on treatment.

  • Avoid 3rd-generation cephalosporins for serious infection even if initially susceptible — risk of on-treatment resistance.
  • Cefepime (stable to AmpC) or a carbapenem are the reliable choices; AmpC is not inhibited by clavulanate.

Carbapenemases — the last-line breakers

Enzymes that hydrolyse carbapenems, defining CRE (Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales). Three families you must know:

CarbapenemaseClassKey point for treatment
KPC (K. pneumoniae carbapenemase)Serine (Ambler A)Inhibited by avibactam & vaborbactam → ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam work
OXA-48Serine (Ambler D)Ceftazidime-avibactam active; vaborbactam less reliable
NDM, VIM, IMP (metallo-β-lactamases)Metallo (Ambler B, zinc-dependent)Not inhibited by avibactam/vaborbactam → need cefiderocol, or ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam
⚠️ Metallo-β-lactamases break the newest inhibitors too

The convenient new β-lactam/β-lactamase-inhibitor combinations (ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam) inhibit the serine carbapenemases (KPC, and avibactam covers OXA-48) but are powerless against metallo-β-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP), which use a zinc mechanism. For NDM you need cefiderocol, or the ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam combination (aztreonam evades the metallo-enzyme; avibactam protects aztreonam from co-existing serine enzymes). Always identify which carbapenemase — the class dictates the drug.

3 · The new anti-CRE agents 💊

  • Ceftazidime-avibactam — KPC and OXA-48 producers; not metallo.
  • Meropenem-vaborbactam — strong for KPC; vaborbactam does not add OXA-48/metallo cover.
  • Imipenem-relebactam — KPC and difficult Pseudomonas.
  • Cefiderocol — a siderophore cephalosporin that hijacks the bacterial iron-uptake system ('Trojan horse') to enter; active against metallo-β-lactamases, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Stenotrophomonas — often the agent of last resort.
  • Ceftolozane-tazobactam — best-in-class for MDR Pseudomonas (not for KPC/CRE).

4 · The Gram-positive MDR organisms 🦠

MRSA — Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus

Resistance from PBP2a (encoded by mecA), an altered penicillin-binding protein that all β-lactams bind poorly — so no standard β-lactam works (the exceptions are the anti-MRSA cephalosporins ceftaroline/ceftobiprole). Treatment:

  • Vancomycin (AUC/MIC 400–600 — see Session 11) or daptomycin for bacteraemia/endocarditis (not for pneumonia — inactivated by surfactant).
  • Linezolid — excellent for MRSA pneumonia and skin/soft-tissue; oral bioavailability ~100%; watch cytopenias, serotonin syndrome with MAOI/SSRI, and neuropathy with prolonged use.
  • Ceftaroline — the β-lactam that binds PBP2a.

VRE — Vancomycin-Resistant Enterococcus

Resistance via vanA/vanB genes that remodel the cell-wall precursor terminus from D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac, so vancomycin can no longer bind — a target-modification mechanism. Treat with linezolid or daptomycin (higher doses for enterococci). Mostly E. faecium. Distinguish colonisation from true infection before treating.

5 · The difficult Gram-negative non-fermenters 🌫️

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa — a resistance polymath combining efflux pumps, porin loss (OprD), AmpC and acquired β-lactamases. Difficult-to-treat resistance (DTR-Pseudomonas) = non-susceptible to all traditional agents (pip-tazo, ceftazidime, cefepime, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones, aztreonam) → use ceftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, imipenem-relebactam or cefiderocol. Do not add a toxic aminoglycoside reflexively when a better β-lactam-based option exists.
  • Acinetobacter baumannii — extreme intrinsic and acquired resistance, OXA-type carbapenemases, efflux. Options are scarce: sulbactam-durlobactam (newer, targeted), high-dose ampicillin-sulbactam, cefiderocol, sometimes polymyxins (colistin) or minocycline. A true 'end of the formulary' organism.
  • Stenotrophomonas maltophilia — intrinsically carbapenem-resistant; treat with co-trimoxazole (first-line) or cefiderocol/levofloxacin.

6 · Clostridioides difficile — the guidance has changed ⚠️

Toxin-mediated colitis after flora disruption (fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, clindamycin, co-amoxiclav are classic triggers). The major update: metronidazole is no longer first-line.

ScenarioPreferred therapy
Initial episode (non-severe or severe)Fidaxomicin (preferred, lower recurrence) or oral vancomycin 125 mg QDS
MetronidazoleOnly if the preferred agents are unavailable, or as adjunct IV in fulminant disease
RecurrenceFidaxomicin, tapered/pulsed vancomycin, bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B monoclonal), consider faecal microbiota transplant for multiple recurrences
Fulminant (ileus, megacolon, shock)High-dose oral/PR vancomycin + IV metronidazole; surgical review
💡 Pearl

The mnemonic has flipped: vancomycin (oral) or fidaxomicin first; metronidazole is the fallback. And oral vancomycin acts locally in the gut — it is not the same as using IV vancomycin for systemic infection.

7 · The master field guide — bug → mechanism → drug 🗺️

Organism / phenotypeResistance mechanismDrug(s) that still work
ESBL EnterobacteralesPlasmid ESBL (CTX-M) hydrolyses 3rd-gen cephalosporinsCarbapenem; cefepime only if low MIC; oral options for cystitis
AmpC producers (ESCPM)Inducible chromosomal β-lactamaseCefepime or carbapenem (avoid 3rd-gen cephalosporins)
CRE — KPCSerine carbapenemaseCeftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam
CRE — OXA-48Serine (class D) carbapenemaseCeftazidime-avibactam; cefiderocol
CRE — NDM/VIM/IMPMetallo-β-lactamase (zinc)Cefiderocol, or ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam
MRSAAltered PBP2a (mecA)Vancomycin, daptomycin (not lung), linezolid, ceftaroline
VRED-Ala-D-Lac cell-wall target change (vanA/B)Linezolid, daptomycin (high dose)
DTR-PseudomonasEfflux + porin (OprD) loss + AmpC/β-lactamasesCeftolozane-tazobactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, imipenem-relebactam, cefiderocol
Acinetobacter (CRAB)OXA carbapenemases, efflux, impermeabilitySulbactam-durlobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam, cefiderocol, colistin
StenotrophomonasIntrinsic metallo + chromosomal β-lactamasesCo-trimoxazole, cefiderocol, levofloxacin
C. difficileToxin production after flora disruptionFidaxomicin or oral vancomycin (metronidazole fallback)

8 · Infection control — the other half of the fight 🧼

Every MDR organism you treat is also a transmission risk. Antibiotics treat the patient; infection control protects the ward.

  • Hand hygiene — the single most effective measure; alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores, so use soap and water for C. diff.
  • Contact precautions & isolation / cohorting for CRE, MRSA, VRE, C. difficile.
  • Active screening surveillance (rectal swabs for CRE/VRE on admission from high-risk settings) to detect silent carriers.
  • Environmental cleaning — sporicidal agents for C. difficile; terminal cleaning of rooms.
  • Antimicrobial stewardship (Sessions 9–10) is itself infection control: reducing selective pressure shrinks the reservoir of resistant organisms.
☠️ M&M — the carbapenem that was the wrong last resort

A 55-year-old repatriated from an overseas ICU grew a Gram-negative rod from blood; flagged carbapenem-resistant, she was escalated to ceftazidime-avibactam as the 'newest, strongest' agent while she deteriorated over 48 hours. The molecular result then returned: an NDM (metallo-β-lactamase). Ceftazidime-avibactam never had a chance — avibactam does not inhibit metallo-enzymes. Precious hours of shock passed on an inactive drug. Only when she was switched to cefiderocol (and the team considered ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam) did she begin to turn. Separately, because she was nursed without contact precautions before the result, a second patient on the unit was later found colonised with the same NDM Klebsiella. Lesson: 'carbapenem-resistant' is not one disease — you must know which carbapenemase, because the class dictates the drug; and the moment you suspect CRE, the isolation and screening must start, not wait for confirmation.

9 · Take-home 🎓

  • Four mechanisms: enzymatic destruction (β-lactamases), target modification (MRSA PBP2a, VRE D-Ala-D-Lac), efflux, porin loss.
  • ESBL → carbapenem for serious infection (MERINO: pip-tazo inferior); cefepime only at low MIC.
  • AmpC (ESCPM) → cefepime or carbapenem, never a 3rd-gen cephalosporin for serious disease.
  • CRE by class: KPC → ceftazidime-avibactam / meropenem-vaborbactam; OXA-48 → ceftazidime-avibactam; NDM/metallo → cefiderocol or ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam.
  • MRSA: vancomycin/linezolid/daptomycin (daptomycin not for lung). VRE: linezolid or daptomycin.
  • C. difficile: fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin first-line — metronidazole is no longer first-line.
  • Identify the exact mechanism, and start infection control early — antibiotics save the patient, isolation saves the ward.

moderatorQs.q: A blood culture is reported as an ESBL E. coli in a septic patient. Why not just use piperacillin–tazobactam, and what do you choose?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because for serious ESBL infection pip-tazo is not reliable. ESBLs (usually CTX-M) hydrolyse penicillins and 3rd-generation cephalosporins, and although tazobactam inhibits the enzyme in vitro, the MERINO randomised trial showed piperacillin–tazobactam was inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia, with higher mortality. So for serious or bacteraemic ESBL disease the answer is a carbapenem (meropenem, or ertapenem if not critically ill). Cefepime is acceptable only when the MIC is low and the infection non-severe. For uncomplicated ESBL cystitis I would spare the carbapenem and use an oral agent such as nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin.

moderatorQs.q: 'Carbapenem-resistant' is on the report. Why is that not enough information to prescribe?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because carbapenem resistance is not one mechanism, and the mechanism dictates the drug. Serine carbapenemases — KPC and OXA-48 — are inhibited by avibactam (and KPC by vaborbactam), so ceftazidime-avibactam or meropenem-vaborbactam work. But metallo-β-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP) use a zinc mechanism that those inhibitors cannot touch — for them you need cefiderocol, or the ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam combination. Resistance can also be non-enzymatic (porin loss plus an ESBL/AmpC). So 'carbapenem-resistant' must be resolved into which carbapenemase before you can pick an active agent — guessing wastes hours of shock on an inactive drug.

moderatorQs.q: Summarise how the treatment of C. difficile has changed and why.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The headline change is that metronidazole is no longer first-line. Current IDSA/SHEA guidance recommends fidaxomicin (preferred, lower recurrence) or oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily for the initial episode, whether non-severe or severe; metronidazole is relegated to a fallback when those are unavailable or as an IV adjunct in fulminant disease. The rationale is superior sustained cure and lower recurrence with the newer approach. For recurrence, options include fidaxomicin, tapered/pulsed vancomycin, the anti-toxin-B monoclonal bezlotoxumab, and faecal microbiota transplant after multiple recurrences. And a practical point: oral vancomycin acts locally in the gut and use soap and water, not alcohol gel, because spores survive alcohol.

audienceQs.q: When can I trust a 3rd-generation cephalosporin against an Enterobacter or Serratia that tested susceptible?
audienceQs.answerHTML: For serious infection, don't. Enterobacter, Serratia and the other AmpC/'ESCPM' organisms carry an inducible chromosomal AmpC β-lactamase that can be de-repressed under β-lactam pressure — so an isolate that looks susceptible to ceftriaxone on day one can emerge resistant on treatment, with clinical failure. The safe choices are cefepime (stable to AmpC) or a carbapenem; and note AmpC is not inhibited by clavulanate, so co-amoxiclav/pip-tazo are unreliable too. Reserve a susceptible-looking 3rd-gen cephalosporin only for low-stakes, non-serious infection where you can monitor and switch.

audienceQs.q: A new admission from an overseas hospital might carry CRE. What do we do before the swabs are back?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Act pre-emptively — don't wait for confirmation. Place the patient in contact precautions in a single room (or cohort with known carriers), send rectal/perirectal screening swabs for CRE (and consider VRE/MRSA per policy), and flag the record so the status follows the patient. Emphasise hand hygiene and dedicated or decontaminated equipment, and ensure environmental cleaning. The M&M cases are exactly this: a colonised repatriated patient nursed without precautions before results seeds a second patient. Early isolation plus active screening is how you stop a single import becoming a ward outbreak — infection control and stewardship together shrink the resistant reservoir.

audienceQs.q: Our MRSA bacteraemia patient developed pneumonia — the team wants to continue daptomycin. Any concern?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes — daptomycin does not work in the lung. It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, so despite excellent activity in bacteraemia and right-sided endocarditis it is ineffective for pneumonia and should not be used to treat it. For MRSA pneumonia switch to linezolid (excellent lung penetration, ~100% oral bioavailability — watch cytopenias, serotonin syndrome and neuropathy) or vancomycin dosed to an AUC/MIC of 400–600. If it is genuinely both a bacteraemia and a pneumonia, pick an agent that covers both sites rather than relying on daptomycin, and confirm source control of the bloodstream focus.
